questions.q: How do you say « I'm cold » ?
questions.why: French treats a bodily state as something you have, so it uses avoir with a bare noun. Je suis froid would describe a cold personality, and il fait froid is the weather, not you.
Beau is an adjective, and an adjective describing the weather needs faire. Il y a only takes a noun with a partitive, as in il y a du soleil.
Avoir mal à plus the body part, with à contracting as usual. French uses the definite article here, never a possessive: j'ai mal à ma tête is wrong.

questions.q: Il a mal ___ dents depuis hier.
questions.why: à + les contracts to aux. Compare j'ai mal au dos, à la gorge, à l'estomac: the contraction follows the gender and number of the body part.

questions.q: How do you say « I'm very hungry » ?
questions.why: The bare noun after avoir behaves like an adjective, so it takes très rather than beaucoup. This is the one place très may stand in front of a noun.

questions.q: Elle joue ___ piano depuis dix ans.
questions.why: Jouer de plus an instrument, and de + le contracts to du. Games and sports take the other preposition: jouer au foot, aux cartes.

questions.q: Which sentence is correct for « She plays tennis and the guitar » ?
choices: Elle joue au tennis et de la guitare
Elle joue du tennis et à la guitare
Elle joue au tennis et à la guitare
Elle joue le tennis et la guitare
questions.why: The preposition splits by category, not by sentence: à for a game or sport, de for an instrument. Neither ever takes a bare definite article after jouer.

questions.q: Il ___ du vent aujourd'hui, ferme la fenêtre.
questions.why: Vent is a noun with a partitive, so both il y a du vent and il fait du vent work. What you cannot do is drop the partitive: il y a vent and il fait vent are both wrong.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT French?
questions.why: Pleuvoir, neiger and geler are complete verbs and need no faire. Il fait pleuvoir would mean he makes it rain; faire is only for the adjectives, as in il fait beau.

questions.q: Je fais ___ vaisselle après le dîner.
questions.why: A named household job takes the definite article: faire la vaisselle, la cuisine, le ménage, les courses. An activity you practise takes the partitive instead: faire du sport, de la natation.
Le dos is masculine, so à + le gives au. The whole frame is avoir mal à, never être mal or avoir de la douleur.

questions.q: Build the sentence: I need to leave.
questions.why: Avoir besoin keeps its de, and what follows de is a bare infinitive. The same shape gives j'ai envie de sortir and j'ai hâte de partir.

questions.q: Build the sentence: We play cards on Sundays.
questions.why: Cards is a game, so jouer à, and à + les gives aux. Le dimanche with the definite article means every Sunday, not this one.

questions.q: The coffee is hot, the weather is hot, and you feel hot. Which set is right?
choices: Le café a chaud / il est chaud / je fais chaud
Le café est chaud / il fait chaud / j'ai chaud
Le café fait chaud / il a chaud / je suis chaud
Le café est chaud / il a chaud / je fais chaud
questions.why: Three subjects, three verbs: an object is chaud with être, the weather with faire, a person with avoir. Je suis chaud never means I feel hot.
Chance is the expression that breaks the bare-noun rule: it keeps its partitive. The negative flattens it to je n'ai pas de chance.

questions.q: Name the three patterns French uses to talk about the weather, with an example of each, and say what goes wrong when they are crossed.
a: 1. il fait + adjective: il fait beau, il fait froid, il fait nuit. 2. il + a weather verb on its own: il pleut, il neige, il gèle. 3. il y a + du / de la / des + noun: il y a du vent, il y a du brouillard, il y a des nuages. Crossing them gives il fait pleuvoir (faire plus a verb), il y a beau (il y a plus an adjective) and il y a vent (the partitive dropped), none of which is French. The overlap is real only for the nouns: il fait du vent and il y a du vent are both said.
questions.why: Each weather word belongs to exactly one frame, and English hides that by saying it is for all three. Knowing which word is an adjective and which is a noun is what picks the frame.
